text: From Apollonius I learned freedom of will and undeviating steadiness of purpose; and to look to nothing else, not even for a moment, except to reason; and to be always the same, in sharp pains, on the occasion of the loss of a child, and in long illness; and to see clearly in a living example that the same man can be both most resolute and yielding, and not peevish in giving his instruction; and to have had before my eyes a man who clearly considered his experience and his skill in expounding philosophical principles as the smallest of his merits; and from him I learned how to receive from friends what are esteemed favours, without being either humbled by them or letting them pass unnoticed.

text: Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil. But I who have seen the nature of the good that it is beautiful, and of the bad that it is ugly, and the nature of him who does wrong, that it is akin to me, not only of the same blood or seed, but that it participates in the same intelligence and the same portion of the divinity, I can neither be injured by any of them, for no one can fix on me what is ugly, nor can I be angry with my kinsman, nor hate him. For we are made for cooperation, like feet, like hands, like eyelids, like the rows of the upper and lower teeth. To act against one another then is contrary to nature; and it is acting against one another to be vexed and to turn away.

text: Men seek retreats for themselves, houses in the country, seashores, and mountains; and thou too art wont to desire such things very much. But this is altogether a mark of the most common sort of men, for it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul, particularly when he has within him such thoughts that by looking into them he is immediately in perfect tranquility; and I affirm that tranquility is nothing else than the good ordering of the mind. Constantly then give to thyself this retreat, and renew thyself; and let thy principles be brief and fundamental, which, as soon as thou shalt recur to them, will be sufficient to cleanse the soul completely, and to send thee back free from all discontent with the things to which thou returnest.

text: Everything which is in any way beautiful is beautiful in itself, and terminates in itself, not having praise as part of itself. Neither worse then nor better is a thing made by being praised. text: Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil.⁠—But consider if it would not be better to say, Do what is necessary, and whatever the reason of the animal which is naturally social requires, and as it requires. tags.when_helps: Someone weighed down by their past who wants to treat the rest of life as a fresh start lived well.

display_text: Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time; and live according to nature the remainder which is allowed thee.
plain: Think of yourself as already dead, your life finished up to now, and live the rest you are given in line with nature.
core_idea: Live the remaining time as a bonus, by nature

text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
note: finding goodness and strength within

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels they have nothing good inside, encouraged to look within for a source that keeps flowing.

display_text: Look within. Within is the fountain of good, and it will ever bubble up, if thou wilt ever dig.
plain: Look within. The source of good is inside you, and it will keep bubbling up if you keep digging.
core_idea: The source of good is within you

text: The art of life is more like the wrestler’s art than the dancer’s, in respect of this, that it should stand ready and firm to meet onsets which are sudden and unexpected.
note: being ready for sudden setbacks

tags.when_helps: Someone shaken by sudden setbacks, wanting to stand firm and ready for whatever comes next.

display_text: The art of life is more like the wrestler’s art than the dancer’s, in respect of this, that it should stand ready and firm to meet onsets which are sudden and unexpected.
plain: Living well is more like wrestling than dancing: you must stand ready and steady to meet sudden, unexpected attacks.
core_idea: Life demands readiness, like wrestling

text: Constantly observe who those are whose approbation thou wishest to have, and what ruling principles they possess. For then thou wilt neither blame those who offend involuntarily, nor wilt thou want their approbation, if thou lookest to the sources of their opinions and appetites.
note: seeking approval from others

tags.when_helps: Someone craving approval from people whose judgement they have never examined.

display_text: Constantly observe who those are whose approbation thou wishest to have, and what ruling principles they possess. For then thou wilt neither blame those who offend involuntarily, nor wilt thou want their approbation, if thou lookest to the sources of their opinions and appetites.
plain: Keep looking at whose approval you want and what principles guide them. Then you won't blame those who offend unintentionally, and you won't crave their approval once you see where their opinions and desires come from.
core_idea: Examine whose approval you seek

text: Every soul, the philosopher says, is involuntarily deprived of truth; consequently in the same way it is deprived of justice and temperance and benevolence and everything of the kind. It is most necessary to bear this constantly in mind, for thus thou wilt be more gentle towards all.
note: being gentle with people's failings

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone angry at others' wrongdoing, who may grow gentler seeing that nobody chooses to miss the truth.

display_text: Every soul, the philosopher says, is involuntarily deprived of truth; consequently in the same way it is deprived of justice and temperance and benevolence and everything of the kind. It is most necessary to bear this constantly in mind, for thus thou wilt be more gentle towards all.
plain: The philosopher says every soul is deprived of truth against its will, and so likewise of justice, self-control, kindness and the rest. Keep this in mind constantly, and you will be gentler with everyone.
core_idea: No one errs willingly; be gentle with all

text: In every pain let this thought be present, that there is no dishonour in it, nor does it make the governing intelligence worse, for it does not damage the intelligence either so far as the intelligence is rational or so far as it is social. Indeed in the case of most pains let this remark of Epicurus aid thee, that pain is neither intolerable nor everlasting, if thou bearest in mind that it has its limits, and if thou addest nothing to it in imagination: and remember this too, that we do not perceive that many things which are disagreeable to us are the same as pain, such as excessive drowsiness, and the being scorched by heat, and the having no appetite. When then thou art discontented about any of these things, say to thyself, that thou art yielding to pain.
note: coping with pain and discomfort

tags.when_helps: Someone in pain or discomfort, reassured that pain has limits and is worsened by what imagination adds.

display_text: In every pain let this thought be present, that there is no dishonour in it, nor does it make the governing intelligence worse, for it does not damage the intelligence either so far as the intelligence is rational or so far as it is social. Indeed in the case of most pains let this remark of Epicurus aid thee, that pain is neither intolerable nor everlasting, if thou bearest in mind that it has its limits, and if thou addest nothing to it in imagination: and remember this too, that we do not perceive that many things which are disagreeable to us are the same as pain, such as excessive drowsiness, and the being scorched by heat, and the having no appetite. plain: Pain is no disgrace and does not harm your mind. As Epicurus said, pain is neither unbearable nor endless if you recall its limits and add nothing to it. Drowsiness, heat and lost appetite are pain too.
core_idea: Pain has limits; don't add to it

plain_judge.issue: Drops "say to thyself that thou art yielding to pain" and the rational and social aspects.

text: Nature has not so mingled the intelligence with the composition of the body, as not to have allowed thee the power of circumscribing thyself and of bringing under subjection to thyself all that is thy own; for it is very possible to be a divine man and to be recognised as such by no one. Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life. And because thou hast despaired of becoming a dialectician and skilled in the knowledge of nature, do not for this reason renounce the hope of being both free and modest and social and obedient to God.
note: disappointed ambitions; goodness without recognition

tags.when_helps: Someone who gave up on a skill or ambition and feels lesser for it, reminded that a good life needs very little.

display_text: Nature has not so mingled the intelligence with the composition of the body, as not to have allowed thee the power of circumscribing thyself and of bringing under subjection to thyself all that is thy own; for it is very possible to be a divine man and to be recognised as such by no one. Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life. And because thou hast despaired of becoming a dialectician and skilled in the knowledge of nature, do not for this reason renounce the hope of being both free and modest and social and obedient to God.
plain: Nature lets you govern what is yours; you can be godlike yet known to no one. Little is needed for a happy life. If you've abandoned hope of great learning, still be free, modest, sociable and obedient to God.
core_idea: Little is needed to live well and nobly

plain_judge.issue: "Do not renounce the hope" of being free becomes a flat command; drops self-circumscription.

text: The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite.
note: living each day well

tags.when_helps: Someone wanting to live each day with steadiness and sincerity, neither frantic nor sluggish.

display_text: The perfection of moral character consists in this, in passing every day as the last, and in being neither violently excited nor torpid nor playing the hypocrite.
plain: Moral perfection is living each day as your last, without frantic excitement, laziness or pretence.
core_idea: Live each day as the last, calmly and honestly

text: It is a ridiculous thing for a man not to fly from his own badness, which is indeed possible, but to fly from other men’s badness, which is impossible.
note: focusing on own faults, not others'

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone consumed by other people's faults, nudged to work on their own instead.

display_text: It is a ridiculous thing for a man not to fly from his own badness, which is indeed possible, but to fly from other men’s badness, which is impossible.
plain: It is absurd to try to escape other people's wrongdoing, which you cannot do, instead of escaping your own, which you can.
core_idea: Flee your own faults, not other people's

text: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to obtain a return?
note: wanting credit or thanks for kindness

tags.when_helps: Someone hurt that their kindness went unthanked or unrewarded.

display_text: When thou hast done a good act and another has received it, why dost thou look for a third thing besides these, as fools do, either to have the reputation of having done a good act or to obtain a return?
plain: Once you have done a good deed and someone has benefited, why want anything more, like a reputation for goodness or something in return? Only fools do that.
core_idea: A good deed needs no reward or recognition

text: On the occasion of every act ask thyself, How is this with respect to me? Shall I repent of it? A little time and I am dead, and all is gone. What more do I seek, if what I am now doing is work of an intelligent living being, and a social being, and one who is under the same law with God?
note: making decisions; avoiding regret

tags.when_helps: Someone weighing a choice who wants to test it against the shortness of life and their values.

display_text: On the occasion of every act ask thyself, How is this with respect to me? Shall I repent of it? A little time and I am dead, and all is gone. What more do I seek, if what I am now doing is work of an intelligent living being, and a social being, and one who is under the same law with God?
plain: Before each action, ask whether you will regret it. Soon you will be dead and everything gone; if you are acting as a thinking, social being under God's law, what more could you want?
core_idea: Act well now; death makes regret pointless

plain_judge.issue: "Under the same law with God" narrowed to "under God's law"; drops "How is this with respect to me?"

text: Thou hast not leisure [or ability] to read. But thou hast leisure [or ability] to check arrogance; thou hast leisure to be superior to pleasure and pain; thou hast leisure to be superior to love of fame, and not to be vexed at stupid and ungrateful people, nay even to care for them.
note: too busy; what remains possible

tags.when_helps: Someone too busy for their usual self-improvement, reminded they can still practise patience and restraint.

display_text: Thou hast not leisure [or ability] to read. But thou hast leisure [or ability] to check arrogance; thou hast leisure to be superior to pleasure and pain; thou hast leisure to be superior to love of fame, and not to be vexed at stupid and ungrateful people, nay even to care for them.
plain: You may not have time to read, but you do have time to curb arrogance, rise above pleasure, pain and fame, and not be annoyed by foolish, ungrateful people, even to care for them.
core_idea: There is always time to improve your character

text: When thou risest from sleep with reluctance, remember that it is according to thy constitution and according to human nature to perform social acts, but sleeping is common also to irrational animals. But that which is according to each individual’s nature is also more peculiarly its own, and more suitable to its nature, and indeed also more agreeable.
note: struggling to get out of bed

tags.when_helps: Someone struggling to get out of bed in the morning, needing a reason to rise and engage.

display_text: When thou risest from sleep with reluctance, remember that it is according to thy constitution and according to human nature to perform social acts, but sleeping is common also to irrational animals. But that which is according to each individual’s nature is also more peculiarly its own, and more suitable to its nature, and indeed also more agreeable.
plain: When you don't want to get up, remember that you are made to do useful work with others; animals sleep too. What fits your own nature is more truly yours and more pleasant.
core_idea: Get up: you were made for work, not sleep

text: Remember that to change thy opinion and to follow him who corrects thy error is as consistent with freedom as it is to persist in thy error. For it is thy own, the activity which is exerted according to thy own movement and judgement, and indeed according to thy own understanding too.
note: admitting a mistake and changing one's mind

tags.when_helps: Someone reluctant to admit a mistake, reassured that accepting correction is itself an act of freedom.

display_text: Remember that to change thy opinion and to follow him who corrects thy error is as consistent with freedom as it is to persist in thy error. For it is thy own, the activity which is exerted according to thy own movement and judgement, and indeed according to thy own understanding too.
plain: Changing your mind when someone corrects you is just as free as sticking to your mistake, because the choice still comes from your own judgement and understanding.
core_idea: Accepting correction is an act of freedom

text: If a thing is in thy own power, why dost thou do it? But if it is in the power of another, whom dost thou blame? The atoms [chance] or the gods? Both are foolish. Thou must blame nobody. For if thou canst, correct that which is the cause; but if thou canst not do this, correct at least the thing itself; but if thou canst not do even this, of what use is it to thee to find fault? For nothing should be done without a purpose.
note: blaming others; fix what you can

tags.when_helps: Someone stuck looking for whom to blame, urged to fix what they can and stop faulting the rest.

display_text: If a thing is in thy own power, why dost thou do it? But if it is in the power of another, whom dost thou blame? The atoms [chance] or the gods? Both are foolish. Thou must blame nobody. For if thou canst, correct that which is the cause; but if thou canst not do this, correct at least the thing itself; but if thou canst not do even this, of what use is it to thee to find fault? For nothing should be done without a purpose.
plain: If something is up to you, why do it badly? If it is up to others, blaming chance or the gods is foolish. Blame nobody: fix the cause or the thing if you can; otherwise complaining is pointless.
core_idea: Blame no one; fix what you can

plain_judge.issue: Adds "badly"; drops "nothing should be done without a purpose".

text: Thou sufferest this justly: for thou choosest rather to become good tomorrow than to be good today.
note: procrastinating on becoming better

tags.when_helps: Someone who keeps postponing becoming better, confronted with the cost of waiting until tomorrow.

display_text: Thou sufferest this justly: for thou choosest rather to become good tomorrow than to be good today.
plain: You deserve what you are suffering, because you would rather become good tomorrow than be good today.
core_idea: Putting off goodness brings its own suffering

text: Receive wealth or prosperity without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.
note: handling success and possible loss

tags.when_helps: Someone enjoying success or wealth, reminded to hold it humbly and loosely.

display_text: Receive wealth or prosperity without arrogance; and be ready to let it go.
plain: Accept wealth and success without arrogance, and be ready to give them up.
core_idea: Hold good fortune lightly

text: If thou didst ever see a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head, lying anywhere apart from the rest of the body, such does a man make himself, as far as he can, who is not content with what happens, and separates himself from others, or does anything unsocial. Suppose that thou hast detached thyself from the natural unity⁠—for thou wast made by nature a part, but now thou hast cut thyself off⁠—yet here there is this beautiful provision, that it is in thy power again to unite thyself. God has allowed this to no other part, after it has been separated and cut asunder, to come together again. But consider the kindness by which he has distinguished man, for he has put it in his power not to be separated at all from the universal; and when he has been separated, he has allowed him to return and to be united and to resume his place as a part.
note: isolation and the chance to reconnect

tags.when_helps: Someone who has cut themselves off from others and fears it is too late, reassured they can return and belong again.

display_text: If thou didst ever see a hand cut off, or a foot, or a head, lying anywhere apart from the rest of the body, such does a man make himself, as far as he can, who is not content with what happens, and separates himself from others, or does anything unsocial. plain: Someone who resents what happens or cuts himself off from others is like a severed limb. Yet God has given people alone the power to rejoin the whole after breaking away, and to take their place again.
core_idea: You can always rejoin the whole you broke from

plain_judge.issue: Drops God's kindness in letting man never be separated at all.

text: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee: but on every occasion ask thyself, What is there in this which is intolerable and past bearing? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess. In the next place remember that neither the future nor the past pains thee, but only the present. But this is reduced to a very little, if thou only circumscribest it, and chidest thy mind, if it is unable to hold out against even this.
note: overwhelmed; taking troubles one moment at a time

tags.when_helps: Someone overwhelmed by imagining all their troubles at once, guided to face only the present moment.

display_text: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life. Let not thy thoughts at once embrace all the various troubles which thou mayest expect to befall thee: but on every occasion ask thyself, What is there in this which is intolerable and past bearing? For thou wilt be ashamed to confess. In the next place remember that neither the future nor the past pains thee, but only the present. plain: Don't trouble yourself by picturing your whole life's troubles at once. Ask what in this moment is truly unbearable. Only the present can hurt you, and taken alone it is small enough to bear.
core_idea: Face only the present moment's trouble

plain_judge.issue: Drops "you will be ashamed to confess" and chiding the mind that cannot hold out.

text: It is not fit that I should give myself pain, for I have never intentionally given pain even to another.
note: harsh self-criticism

tags.when_helps: Someone tormenting themselves with self-blame, invited to treat themselves as gently as they treat others.

display_text: It is not fit that I should give myself pain, for I have never intentionally given pain even to another.
plain: I should not cause myself pain, since I have never deliberately caused pain even to anyone else.
core_idea: Don't hurt yourself more than you'd hurt others

text: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgement now.
note: distress caused by our own judgements

tags.when_helps: Someone pained by an outside event, reminded that the pain lies in their judgement, which they can change.

display_text: If thou art pained by any external thing, it is not this thing that disturbs thee, but thy own judgement about it. And it is in thy power to wipe out this judgement now.
plain: When something outside you causes you pain, it is not the thing that disturbs you but your judgement of it, and you can erase that judgement right now.
core_idea: Your judgement, not events, causes your distress

text: Remember that the ruling faculty is invincible, when self-collected it is satisfied with itself, if it does nothing which it does not choose to do, even if it resist from mere obstinacy. What then will it be when it forms a judgement about anything aided by reason and deliberately? Therefore the mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure to which he can fly for, refuge and for the future be inexpugnable. He then who has not seen this is an ignorant man; but he who has seen it and does not fly to this refuge is unhappy.
note: the calm mind as an inner refuge

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling under siege who needs a sense of an inner refuge nothing outside can breach.

display_text: Remember that the ruling faculty is invincible, when self-collected it is satisfied with itself, if it does nothing which it does not choose to do, even if it resist from mere obstinacy. What then will it be when it forms a judgement about anything aided by reason and deliberately? Therefore the mind which is free from passions is a citadel, for man has nothing more secure to which he can fly for refuge and for the future be inexpugnable. He then who has not seen this is an ignorant man; but he who has seen it and does not fly to this refuge is unhappy.
plain: The mind that keeps its own counsel cannot be conquered. A mind free of passions is a fortress, the safest refuge a person has. Not seeing this is ignorance; seeing it and not using it is misery.
core_idea: A calm mind is an unconquerable fortress

plain_judge.issue: Drops even obstinate resistance and the stronger case of judgement aided by reason.

text: Say nothing more to thyself than what the first appearances report. Suppose that it has been reported to thee that a certain person speaks ill of thee. This has been reported; but that thou hast been injured, that has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. I do see; but that he is in danger, I do not see. Thus then always abide by the first appearances, and add nothing thyself from within, and then nothing happens to thee.
note: catastrophising; not adding to the bare facts

tags.when_helps: Someone spiralling from bad news into imagined worst cases, guided to stay with only the facts.

display_text: Say nothing more to thyself than what the first appearances report. Suppose that it has been reported to thee that a certain person speaks ill of thee. This has been reported; but that thou hast been injured, that has not been reported. I see that my child is sick. I do see; but that he is in danger, I do not see. Thus then always abide by the first appearances, and add nothing thyself from within, and then nothing happens to thee.
plain: Tell yourself only what you actually observe. If someone speaks ill of you, that is the fact; that you were harmed is not. Add nothing from inside, and nothing has happened to you.
core_idea: Stick to the facts; add no story

plain_judge.issue: Drops the sick-child example.

text: A cucumber is bitter.⁠—Throw it away.⁠—There are briars in the road.⁠—Turn aside from them.⁠—This is enough. Do not add, And why were such things made in the world?
note: dealing with annoyances without complaining

tags.when_helps: Someone annoyed by small obstacles, encouraged to deal with them simply instead of asking why they exist.

display_text: A cucumber is bitter.⁠—Throw it away.⁠—There are briars in the road.⁠—Turn aside from them.⁠—This is enough. Do not add, And why were such things made in the world?
plain: If a cucumber is bitter, throw it away. If there are thorns on the path, step around them. That is enough; don't ask why such things exist in the world.
core_idea: Deal with annoyances; don't ask why they exist

text: Neither in thy actions be sluggish nor in thy conversation without method, nor wandering in thy thoughts, nor let there be in thy soul inward contention nor external effusion, nor in life be so busy as to have no leisure.
note: balance; busyness and scattered thoughts

tags.when_helps: Someone scattered and over-busy who wants more focus, calm and space in their days.

display_text: Neither in thy actions be sluggish nor in thy conversation without method, nor wandering in thy thoughts, nor let there be in thy soul inward contention nor external effusion, nor in life be so busy as to have no leisure.
plain: Don't be sluggish in what you do, muddled in what you say, or scattered in what you think; don't let your soul be torn inside or spill outward, and don't be too busy for leisure.
core_idea: Live with focus, order and calm

text: Suppose that men kill thee, cut thee in pieces, curse thee. What then can these things do to prevent thy mind from remaining pure, wise, sober, just? For instance, if a man should stand by a limpid pure spring, and curse it, the spring never ceases sending up potable water; and if he should cast clay into it or filth, it will speedily disperse them and wash them out, and will not be at all polluted. How then shalt thou possess a perpetual fountain and not a mere well? By forming thyself hourly to freedom conjoined with contentment, simplicity and modesty.
note: staying clear and good under insult

tags.when_helps: Someone attacked or cursed by others, reassured that their mind can remain clear like a spring that washes out filth.

display_text: Suppose that men kill thee, cut thee in pieces, curse thee. What then can these things do to prevent thy mind from remaining pure, wise, sober, just? For instance, if a man should stand by a limpid pure spring, and curse it, the spring never ceases sending up potable water; and if he should cast clay into it or filth, it will speedily disperse them and wash them out, and will not be at all polluted. How then shalt thou possess a perpetual fountain and not a mere well? By forming thyself hourly to freedom conjoined with contentment, simplicity and modesty.
plain: Even if people kill or curse you, they cannot stop your mind being pure and just, as a spring stays clean when cursed or dirtied. Become such a fountain by daily practising freedom, contentment, simplicity and modesty.
core_idea: No one can pollute a mind that renews itself

text: Dost thou wish to be praised by a man who curses himself thrice every hour? Wouldst thou wish to please a man who does not please himself? Does a man please himself who repents of nearly everything that he does?
note: seeking approval from unhappy people

tags.when_helps: Someone anxious for the praise of people who are unhappy with themselves.

display_text: Dost thou wish to be praised by a man who curses himself thrice every hour? Wouldst thou wish to please a man who does not please himself? Does a man please himself who repents of nearly everything that he does?
plain: Why would you want praise from someone who curses himself constantly, or to please someone who isn't pleased with himself and regrets almost everything he does?
core_idea: Don't seek approval from the self-dissatisfied

text: To my own free will the free will of my neighbour is just as indifferent as his poor breath and flesh. For though we are made especially for the sake of one another, still the ruling power of each of us has its own office, for otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be my harm, which God has not willed in order that my unhappiness may not depend on another.
note: others' bad behaviour need not ruin our happiness

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone whose happiness feels hostage to another person's bad behaviour.

display_text: To my own free will the free will of my neighbour is just as indifferent as his poor breath and flesh. For though we are made especially for the sake of one another, still the ruling power of each of us has its own office, for otherwise my neighbour’s wickedness would be my harm, which God has not willed in order that my unhappiness may not depend on another.
plain: My neighbour's will matters as little to my own will as his body does. We exist for one another, but each mind has its own work; God did not let my happiness depend on someone else's wickedness.
core_idea: Another's wrongdoing cannot harm your mind

text: He who fears death either fears the loss of sensation or a different kind of sensation. But if thou shalt have no sensation, neither wilt thou feel any harm; and if thou shalt acquire another kind of sensation, thou wilt be a different kind of living being and thou wilt not cease to live.
note: fear of death

tags.when_helps: Someone afraid of death who wants a calm, reasoned way to think about it.

display_text: He who fears death either fears the loss of sensation or a different kind of sensation. But if thou shalt have no sensation, neither wilt thou feel any harm; and if thou shalt acquire another kind of sensation, thou wilt be a different kind of living being and thou wilt not cease to live.
plain: Fearing death means fearing either no sensation or a different kind. If you feel nothing, nothing can hurt you; if you feel something different, you become another kind of living being and keep living.
core_idea: Death, either way, is nothing to fear

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them.
note: patience with difficult people

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone exasperated with other people, given a simple choice: teach them or bear with them.

display_text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them.
plain: People exist for each other, so either teach them or put up with them.
core_idea: Teach others or bear with them

text: He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.
note: temptation to do wrong; it harms oneself

tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on wrongdoing, theirs or another's, who may see that it chiefly harms the doer.

display_text: He who does wrong does wrong against himself. He who acts unjustly acts unjustly to himself, because he makes himself bad.
plain: Whoever does wrong wrongs himself, because by acting unjustly he makes himself a worse person.
core_idea: Wrongdoing harms the wrongdoer most

text: Thy present opinion founded on understanding, and thy present conduct directed to social good, and thy present disposition of contentment with everything which happens⁠—that is enough.
note: feeling not enough; the present suffices

tags.when_helps: Someone who feels they must always do or have more, reminded that the present can be enough.

display_text: Thy present opinion founded on understanding, and thy present conduct directed to social good, and thy present disposition of contentment with everything which happens⁠—that is enough.
plain: Right now, a judgement based on understanding, actions aimed at the common good, and contentment with whatever happens: that is enough.
core_idea: Good judgement, good acts, contentment suffice

note: patience and kindness toward wrongdoers

tags.when_helps: Someone angry at a wrongdoer they cannot correct, encouraged to show patience and kindness instead.
